blocks.title: You'll want to know: いっぱい

segments.text: いっぱい — ippai — "full", as a cup is full, or as you are after a big meal. It also means "a lot": a lot of people, a lot of work.

Four beats: i–p–pa–i. い, the small っ that holds a beat, and the last い you already write. The third sign is は with the small circle at its upper right, and that circle makes a p: ha becomes pa. The next lesson writes it.

segments.text: は ha + ゜ becomes ぱ pa.

Write は in full, in the order you learned it. Then add the small circle of the handakuten at the upper right, where the voicing mark would go. Keep it small and open, and do not let it touch the sign.
The circle works only on the h row, and it always makes a p: ha becomes pa. You saw it on ほ for ぽ, in いっぽん.
With いっ in front and い after it, you can now write the word from the last lesson: いっぱい, ippai, full.
Write は, then ば, then ぱ, and say ha, ba, pa.
Write ほ ぼ ぽ and は ば ぱ (pa) in rows, and say each one.
Write いっぱい from memory and say ippai.
Stop after one accurate form.
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart.

feedback.correct: Right: は with the small circle is ぱ, read pa.

segments.text: ひ hi + ゜ becomes ぴ pi.
Write ひ in full: one stroke, a short rise, the deep bowl, and up again. Then add the small circle at the upper right, beside the end of the stroke. Keep it small and open.
The circle makes a p again: hi becomes pi. The voicing mark on the same sign gives び, bi, so one base sign now has three readings.
With えん in front and つ after it, you can now write the word from the last lesson: えんぴつ, enpitsu, a pencil.
Write ひ, then び, then ぴ, and say hi, bi, pi.
Write は ぱ and ひ ぴ (pi) in pairs, and say each one.
Write えんぴつ from memory and say enpitsu.
Stop after one accurate form.
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: いっぴき

segments.text: いっぴき — ippiki — "one small animal": one cat, one dog, one fish. Japanese counts animals with a word of their own, the way it counts long thin things with いっぽん.
The new sign is spent at once. い, a small っ, ぴ and き: four beats, i–p–pi–ki. The small っ holds a beat before the p, as it does in いっぱい (ippai). You write every sign in it now.

segments.text: ふ fu + ゜ becomes ぷ pu.
Write ふ in full, in the order you learned it. Then add the small circle at the upper right, above the dot on the right. Keep it small and open.
The sign is read pu. The f of fu goes, and the lips close for a p. With the voicing mark the same sign gives ぶ, bu.
With きっ in front of it, you can now write the word from the last lesson: きっぷ, kippu, a ticket.
Write ふ, then ぶ, then ぷ, and say fu, bu, pu.
Write ぱ (pa), ぴ (pi), ぷ (pu) and ぽ, and say each one.
Write きっぷ from memory and say kippu.
Stop after one accurate form.
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart.

The new sign is spent at once. て and ん, then ぷ and ら: four beats, te–n–pu–ra. After ん the p comes out clearly, as in しんぱい (shinpai). You write every sign in it now.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: ぺらぺら

segments.text: ぺらぺら — perapera — "fluent, fluently": it says that someone speaks a language with ease. It is one of the many doubled words Japanese uses for a sound or a manner: pera, and pera again.
Four beats: pe–ra–pe–ra. ら you already write. The other sign, twice, is へ with the small circle, so he becomes pe. The next lesson writes it.

segments.text: へ he + ゜ becomes ぺ pe.
Write へ in full: one stroke, up to the low peak and down to the right. Then add the small circle at the upper right, above the long way down. Keep it small and open.
The circle makes a p: he becomes pe. With it you write every sign of the p row: ぱ (pa) ぴ (pi) ぷ (pu) ぺ ぽ.
With ら after it, twice over, you can now write the word from the last lesson: ぺらぺら, perapera, fluent.
Write へ, then べ, then ぺ, and say he, be, pe.
Write ぱ (pa) ぴ (pi) ぷ (pu) ぺ (pe) ぽ in order, and say each one.
Write ぺらぺら from memory and say perapera.
Stop after one accurate form.
Source: Unicode Hiragana chart.
